hero.subline: for Generation Z & Alpha — knowledgeable and safe in the digital environment
hero.body: Z & Alpha Initiative is a pioneering project in Vietnam, dedicated to enhancing digital awareness, digital skills, and mental well-being for young people in the technology era. We believe that a healthy digital world can only be built when the younger generations are equipped with deep knowledge, empathy, and enduring human values.

about.metaTitle: About Z & Alpha — The Great Rewiring of Childhood
about.heroBody: As children move from an experience-based childhood to a screen-based one, their entire developmental environment has been rewired. This is the context, the problem, and the solution direction that the Z & Alpha Initiative pursues.
about.s1Body: In a 2024 study analysing the impact of social media and smartphones on the psycho-social development of children and adolescents in the US and other developed countries, Jonathan Haidt — Professor of social psychology at NYU's Stern School of Business and PhD in social psychology from the University of Pennsylvania — introduced the concept of “The Great Rewiring of Childhood”: a complete restructuring of childhood as children shift from a development environment grounded in real-world experience to one mediated through screens.
about.s1VnContext: Vietnam is among the countries where this “rewiring of childhood” is unfolding extremely fast: social-media use among young people is near-universal, with heavy dependence on mobile devices. Three defining traits of the digital environment Vietnam's young generation is growing up in:

traits.title: Digital-first social interaction
traits.en: Tương tác qua nền tảng số

traits.title: Blurred digital–physical boundaries
traits.en: Ranh giới thực – ảo ngày càng mờ

about.s1Bridge: Vietnam sits squarely on the trajectory Haidt describes, but with greater intensity due to its “mobile-first society”. The impact does not stop at content — it is an entire ecosystem shaping children's behaviour, psychology and social development.

directImpacts.term: Lack of protection in the digital world

indirectImpacts.term: Provides ideal infrastructure for fraudulent behaviour
A digital-literacy gap between knowing how to use and knowing how to protect oneself

about.s1Quote: A childhood lived on a screen cannot nurture a healthy, fully developed human being.

challenges.title: The challenge of social media's business model
challenges.body: Social media does not compete on content — users' “attention” is the resource being exploited. Children, whose brains have not yet developed full attentional self-control, become the “optimisation target”, easily steered by this business model. This produces many long-term consequences for the brain development and mental health of the young generation.

challenges.title: The challenge of social cooperation
challenges.body: Many people see the problem and feel something is wrong and needs to change, yet no one dares to change alone for fear of disadvantage if others don't follow, or of criticism. The clearest example is parents: they clearly see social media's harm to their children, yet for many reasons still allow them to use it. In Vietnam, where parents have a strong sense of social competition, this challenge is even more pronounced.

challenges.title: The challenge of governance & digital-skill provisioning
challenges.body: Given the nature of social media, teaching young people merely to “know how to use it” is not enough. Even those who “know how to use it” can still become addicted, and can still fall into traps of psychological and behavioural manipulation. We therefore need to broaden the concept of “digital skills” beyond knowledge or technique, coordinated with synchronised governance mechanisms and policy regulation.

about.s2Quote: We are overprotecting children in the real world while underprotecting them online.

solutions.title: Establish regulation and policy
solutions.body: Solving the problems caused by social media cannot rest solely on each child learning to limit their own use, or on parents spending more time managing their children's time online — still less on expecting platform companies to throttle their own money-making machines. It must originate from regulation and policy set by state authorities, coordinated enforcement and oversight through educational institutions, combined with guidance and mentoring from parents.

solutions.title: Make “digital skills” a core competency
solutions.body: “Digital skills” — including how to use, and how one should use, social media — should be classified as essential competencies, provided to adolescents through family, school and society. Even parents, who belong to a generation that grew up without social media, should be encouraged to learn and absorb this knowledge so they can accompany their children toward healthy growth in today's digital world.

solutions.title: Redesign the development environment
solutions.body: The problem social media brings does not come from any single platform — we are facing the fact that the entire “ecosystem of childhood” has changed. To resolve the mental-health crisis while keeping the benefits social media offers, we must redesign the educational, play and family environments. Children develop healthily through free play, social interaction within safe bounds, face-to-face communication and encouraged independent exploration.

about.s3Quote: Children grow up through experiences in the real world.

activitiesEducation.title: Education programmes
activitiesEducation.lead: The Z & Alpha Initiative works with educational institutions to run knowledge-sharing programmes, digital-skills training and real-world experiential activities that help reduce the influence of social media.
activitiesEducation.pillarsTitle: Our education model rests on three core pillars
activitiesEducation.pillar1Title: Awareness of digital technology and mental health
activitiesEducation.pillar1Body: Helps young people understand how persuasive technology shapes behaviour and mental health — so they choose actively instead of being steered.
activitiesEducation.pillar2Body: Building a comprehensive digital skill set within the UNESCO Asia-Pacific “digital literacy” competency framework.
activitiesEducation.pillar3Body: Designing visual, hands-on activities — such as science education, art education and extended reading — to reduce dependence on social media.
activitiesEducation.chtTitle: Awareness of digital technology & mental health
activitiesEducation.chtMod1Body: Why do tech companies fight for our attention? How does that value shape the design of the products we use every day? How do the financial incentives behind these products harm us and society? Once students grasp these key points, they realise what they can do to push for a technology that genuinely serves the best interests of people.
activitiesEducation.chtMod2Body: Explore how the sophisticated designs inside every social-media product manipulate you to capture attention and change human behaviour.
activitiesEducation.chtMod3Body: Our minds and bodies have vulnerabilities that can be exploited. Persuasive technology targets exactly those weaknesses, pushing us to keep clicking, scrolling and interacting endlessly. Once students understand how persuasive technology exploits our weaknesses, they realise that social-media companies are neglecting their duty of care for users' health and well-being.
activitiesEducation.chtMod4Body: Once we understand the harms of persuasive technology and the systemic forces driving it, we can begin to imagine how to build a world based on humane technology — a technology that operates for the common good of everyone.
activitiesEducation.skillsLead: The Z & Alpha Initiative builds, or co-builds, training programmes, courses and activities to help adolescents develop the digital skill set within the “digital literacy” competency framework developed by the UNESCO Asia-Pacific office in cooperation with relevant stakeholders.

activitiesEducation.altTitle: Designing educational activities focused on visual, hands-on interaction as an alternative to social-media use
activitiesEducation.altArtBody: Art education does not only teach creative skills — it is also a space where children and adolescents can express emotions that ordinary language sometimes cannot capture. When they draw, write, perform or make something with their own hands, young people get a chance to process emotions, relieve stress and build a sense of self-mastery — foundational elements of healthy mental well-being. In a context where screens and social media increasingly crowd out real experiences, art offers a deep, intentional form of presence — a necessary counterweight to the digital world that dominates young people's lives.
activitiesEducation.altReadingBody: Reading is one of the least expensive activities yet brings some of the most far-reaching benefits for the brain — from expanding vocabulary and strengthening focus, to developing critical thinking and imagination. Especially for a generation growing up in a digital environment, the reading habit is also an intentional form of "screen detox" — letting the brain rest from the constant stimulation of social media and recover the deep focus that is gradually being eroded.
activitiesEducation.altScienceBody: Science education awakens something immensely precious in young people: curiosity. When a child asks "why?" and is guided to find the answer themselves, they not only learn about the natural world but also experience the pure joy of discovery — a feeling far deeper and more lasting than the instant stimulation social media provides. Science also teaches children to face an uncertain future with composure: that failure is part of the process, that the question matters more than the answer — thinking lessons that build strength of will.
activitiesEducation.inviteBody: We believe that to create real change for the young generation, no single organisation can act alone. We therefore sincerely invite schools, civil-society organisations, businesses and media agencies to join hands in this initiative. Whether by co-running activities, sharing expertise, connecting communities or supporting communications — every form of collaboration helps build an education ecosystem strong enough to protect the mental health and healthy development of Vietnam's children and adolescents in the digital age.

activitiesPolicy.title: Policy recommendations
activitiesPolicy.lead: Evidence-based policy proposals and recommendations for schools, parents and regulatory bodies.
activitiesPolicy.featuredTitle: Social media and the mental health of children and adolescents: An urgent issue requiring action
activitiesPolicy.contextP1: In the digital era, social media has become inseparable from the lives of children and adolescents. Beyond communication and entertainment, it now shapes identity, supports career development and builds social relationships.
activitiesPolicy.contextP2: Yet the prevalence of social media also brings concerning negative impacts — especially on mental health, attention for learning, and the holistic development of young people. Manifestations such as social anxiety, image pressure, FOMO and cyberbullying are increasingly common.
activitiesPolicy.intlLead: Many countries have rolled out decisive policy to protect adolescents in the digital environment.
activitiesPolicy.intl1Body: Parliament passed a law banning under-16s from using social media, slated to apply from December 2025, with fines up to AUD 50 million for non-compliant platforms.
activitiesPolicy.intl2Body: From March 2026, students from primary through high school are banned from using smartphones in classrooms.
activitiesPolicy.intl3Body: Parliament is proposing a ban on social media for under-15s following a thorough inquiry into the negative effects of digital platforms.
activitiesPolicy.vnBody: Initial studies and forums have documented the impact of social media on adolescent mental health. However, there is still a lack of empirical data, concrete scientific evidence and clear policy recommendations for parents, schools, regulators and technology platforms.
activitiesPolicy.goalsLead: The conference is organised to create an academic and policy forum to:
activitiesPolicy.goal1: Share international experience and existing research findings.
activitiesPolicy.goal3: Propose policy, education and communication solutions to protect mental health for children and adolescents in the digital environment.

activitiesPolicy.discussion2: What are the priority actions for the next 5–10 years?
activitiesPolicy.discussion3: How can we strengthen cross-sector coordination between the state, schools, families, society and technology platforms?
